Gallagher says no sole reason for yesterday's interest rate rise
Finance Minister Katy Gallagher has been keen to emphasise there are a range of factors contributing to yesterday's interest rate rise.
Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock said yesterday's interest rate increase was because public and private demand remained too high across the economy.
The government has been under pressure to cut spending, and has flagged savings in the mid-year fiscal and economic outlook in December.
Asked in the parliamentary press gallery whether the government spending was behind the demand, Gallagher says there

"There's a number of different things going on. I know everyone wants to point finger and find a sole blame or a sole reason for it," Gallagher says."I think there are a number of reasons and the war in the Middle East is not helping because that is not only flowing through to petrol prices, the price of oil, but it's having other supply shocks on the economy."
"There's a number of different things going on. I know everyone wants to point finger and find a sole blame or a sole reason for it," Gallagher says.

"I think there are a number of reasons and the war in the Middle East is not helping because that is not only flowing through to petrol prices, the price of oil, but it's having other supply shocks on the economy."
One Nation calls for efficiency in capital spending
One Nation MP David Farley has said improving efficiency in major projects, rather than cutting spending, is key to dealing with the country's inflation woes.
"It's not so much spending cuts, I think. It's more about being efficient with spending itself," he told ABC Radio National Breakfast.
He highlighted the Snowy Hydro 2.0 project, which has ballooned to more than 12 times its initial cost to $25 billion.

"We're midway through a lot of major projects at the moment. It's either abandon those projects and write that capital off, or take a breath and say, rightio, why are we being so inefficient in this capital spending? What's the cause of it? And get it under control."
Farley said the government should tackle fraud in the National Disability Insurance Scheme rather than cutting services.
He was also asked about water policy, an important issue for his regional electorate of Farrer, following the NSW government's increased allocations for the Murrumbidgee.
"Murrumbidgee increases at 2 per cent. That's a plastic bucket full, to be quite honest with you. It's not enough."
'Literally holidaying' British backpackers should work in regional areas, One Nation MP says
One Nation MP David Farley has said British backpackers should never be allowed to dodge regional work requirements.

The PM met with his UK counterpart Andy Burnham on the sidelines of CHOGM in the Caribbean this week to discuss possible changes to a Morrison-era free trade deal with the UK that allowed British backpackers to live in Australia for up to three years without meeting any specific work requirements.
Other nationals on Working Holiday Maker visas have had to do a stint in regional areas to extend their time here, and Farley said the same should go for British backpackers.
"Now, if that was the case, we wouldn't have them congregating around the Gold Coast and Bondi and Torquay and places like that," Farley told ABC Radio National Breakfast.
"We're paying the price of that now. We went from roughly 40,000 backpackers up to 80,000, literally holidaying for three years and turning themselves into coffee baristas.
"We need that workforce, and especially that age group of workforce, in regional Australia."
A read-out from the bilateral meeting between Albanese and Burnham did not mention the backpacker issue, which has become a contentious issue amid an ongoing migration debate.
Regional Australia a 'tinderbox', One Nation MP says
One Nation MP David Farley, who represents the regional electorate of Farrer, has said an "abhorrent" alleged attack on one of the party's volunteers in Victoria is "not in our culture".
Yesterday, One Nation leader Pauline Hanson said the 60-year-old man suffered a brain bleed after allegedly being assaulted with a baseball bat in Torquay over the weekend.
"An attack like this is abhorrent. It's not something that our democracy needs ... and it's definitely something that's not in our culture," Farley told ABC Radio National Breakfast.

He said the party has real concerns about the safety of its staff and candidates, and said the government needed to engage more with communities in the agricultural belt, especially on environmental policies.

"In regional Australia, in particular, there's a lot of discontent and disenfranchised people," he said."Society at the moment is kind of like a tinderbox ... it takes very little to spark, a little spark to put anyone over the edge."

Gallagher says budget 'needs to look after people'
The finance minister has responded to the Reserve Bank governor's warning that sluggish inflation will make Australians feel like they're in a recession.
Yesterday, Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock said that while she didn't see Australia's economy falling into a recession, growth will slow "markedly".
"It shows that inflation is quite sluggish, and I think that is going to … make people feel like it's a recession because they feel poorer," Bullock said yesterday.
But Katy Gallagher told ABC Radio National Breakfast that wasn't included in the bank's forecasts.
"I think our focus has to be on the decisions we make, making sure that our decisions contribute positively to the fight against inflation," Gallagher says.
She says the budget "needs to look after people" and that it needs to invest in Medicare, social security and disability services.
Coalition tells government to 'make the tough decisions'
Nationals senator Bridget McKenzie has accused the government of trying to "wash their hands" of blame over rising inflation and interest rates.
The Reserve Bank yesterday lifted interest rates to an 18-year high due to rising inflation figures.
"High inflation hits the poorest the most," McKenzie said on Sunrise, on a panel alongside Housing Minister Clare O'Neil.
McKenzie said the government had a "level of denial" about "who is responsible for the terrible situation that Australians find themselves in".
"Empathetic statements don't help fix this problem that the Labor party created. Making the tough decisions in a budget does," she said."They need to not spend more than they save."
"Empathetic statements don't help fix this problem that the Labor party created. Making the tough decisions in a budget does," she said.
"They need to not spend more than they save."
Housing minister says cutting government spending must be done carefully
Housing Minister Clare O'Neil said yesterday's interest rate rise was another blow to families who are feeling "frustrated and frankly exhausted" by the current economic environment.
The Reserve Bank lifted interest rates to an 18-year high of 4.85 per cent after figures released last week showed inflation rising to 4.3 per cent.
"This is a really tough moment for the country," she said on Sunrise.
She said the government had worked to bring inflation down post-COVID, but the war in Iran and the AI boom, as well as domestic pressures, had seen it rise again.

She said the government had a clear plan to: first, "bring back government spending"; second, continue giving cost-of-living relief without adding to inflation, which she said was a "delicate balancing act"; and third, address productivity problems.
"Whenever you hear politicians talking about cutting government spending, remember, that's services that families at home are relying on. And that's why this has to be done carefully."
She said the government would give a budget update outlining new measures before Christmas.
Wilson says Labor's private health rebate savings is 'false economics'
Tim Wilson has pushed back on the suggestion the Coalition is trying to block savings measures, such as winding back the over-65s private health rebate.
Labor wants to bring the rebate in line with the concession other Australians get in a measure that would save $3 billion over four years.
This morning, Finance Minister Katy Gallagher accused the Coalition and parliament of blocking the government's savings measures.
Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, Wilson says the government's savings are "false economics".
"People consume most of their health care expenditure in the latter stages of their life. We need more older Australians taking up private health insurance, not fewer," Wilson says.

"If you do, you're pushing more costs onto the taxpayer. This is just Labor trying to find a pathway to target older Australians again, rather than focusing on what will bring the budget sustainably back into a position and more importantly drive a private sector growth."
Wilson says government won't admit to nature of persistent inflation
Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson says the government is "addicted to spending" and blamed Labor for yesterday's rate rise.
Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock blamed high public and private demand across the country for the interest rate rise.
Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, Wilson says Labor is talking about savings while saying there's no link between public spending and inflation.
Wilson says he's concerned interest rates will remain high for the next calendar year.
"The government isn't prepared to admit the nature of the problem and therefore outline the pathway to address it and to get inflation pressure down and interest rates down," Wilson says.
Minister lays blame at Coalition, parliament for not backing savings measures
The finance minister has laid blame on the Coalition and parliament for not supporting the government's savings measures in parliament.
Labor has attempted to wind back the private health insurance rebate for over-65s to bring it in line with rebates for people in other age groups.
The Coalition has opposed the measures, and the government doesn't have a majority in the upper house to pass the measures alone.
Katy Gallagher told ABC Radio National Breakfast that the government gets "a lot of free advice" about cutting spending, but savings measures aren't supported in parliament.

"We take modest ideas to the parliament, they're rejected. So let's be clear that this cutting government spending idea is responsibility on the parliament to help in that," Gallagher says."At the moment, that's not what they're doing. They are blocking sensible savings ... They don't actually come up with where they would like to cut."
"We take modest ideas to the parliament, they're rejected. So let's be clear that this cutting government spending idea is responsibility on the parliament to help in that," Gallagher says.
"At the moment, that's not what they're doing. They are blocking sensible savings ... They don't actually come up with where they would like to cut."
Gallagher says Labor wants to contribute 'positively' to inflation fight
Finance Minister Katy Gallagher says the government wants to ensure that it is contributing "positively" to the fight against inflation.
Yesterday, the Reserve Bank of Australia hiked interest rates for the fifth time this year to 4.85 per cent. It's the highest cash rate since late 2008.
The central bank's governor, Michele Bullock, blamed high public and private demand across the country for the rate rise.
The government has flagged budget savings in its upcoming mid-year fiscal and economic outlook in December.
"Our job is to do what we can to make sure that we're contributing positively to that fight against inflation," Gallagher tells ABC Radio National Breakfast.
"Similar to the decisions we've taken in previous budgets, our job will be to look at where we can find savings across the budget and still invest in the things that Australians expect us to do."
Australia and UK release joint statement denouncing 'toxic online environment'
Australia and the United Kingdom have vowed to address a "toxic" online environment, saying it erodes democracies and deters talented people from entering public life.

Both countries have committed to holding a forum next year to bring together technology, expertise and practical solutions to help protect parliamentarians from online abuse, according to a joint statement released during the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in the Caribbean.

"We know that in Australia and the UK women parliamentarians are three times more likely to report receiving sexualised or gender-based threats, online and in person, than men in parliament," the statement said."And in the UK and Australia, elected representatives have been killed or injured for doing their jobs, out in their communities."

"We know that in Australia and the UK women parliamentarians are three times more likely to report receiving sexualised or gender-based threats, online and in person, than men in parliament," the statement said.
"And in the UK and Australia, elected representatives have been killed or injured for doing their jobs, out in their communities."
The statement comes after Independent MP Helen Haines lost both her legs in an alleged attack last month. In the UK, politicians Jo Cox and Sir David Amess were killed in 2016 and 2021, respectively.
The statement said that software tools are being trialled in both parliaments and that addressing harms requires collective action, respectful debate and a change in attitudes.
'Good' that consensus has been reached on slavery apology, Albanese says
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has welcomed consensus on a UK apology for slavery.
Millions of Africans were stolen from their homes during the transatlantic slave trade between the 15th and 19th centuries.
UK PM Andy Burnham has left the door open to an apology, although reparations are unlikely.
"We understand slavery was a practice that is abhorrent. What is happening now in 2027 is an appropriate response, which is to have that respectful dialogue, and that's a good thing," Albanese says.
"At the last CHOGM meeting that was held two years ago there was not a consensus there. It's good that a consensus has been reached."
PM defends govt measures as 'providing support'
The prime minister has pushed back on the suggestions that measures like the government household battery scheme should be means tested to reign in spending.
There have been growing calls, including from the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry, to means test the electric vehicle and home batteries schemes.
Anthony Albanese says Labor's cheaper home batteries program, which allows households and businesses to install discounted batteries, is "providing support".
He's defended the government's cost-of-living measures, such as cheaper PBS medicines and fuel excise cuts.
"Every measure that we did, was aimed at take that that's aimed at taking pressure off the health budget and making sure it helps individuals," Albanese says.
PM says govt won't 'rip money' out of health, schools in savings package
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says yesterday's rate rise confirms the government's decision to look for savings before the end of the year.
Labor has flagged it will find savings measures in the mid-year economic and fiscal outlook due to be released in December.
Albanese has accused the Coalition of opposing savings measures before parliament, including a private health insurance rebate for over-65s.

"A range of savings that we have put forward have been rejected by the Coalition, and a range of expenditures have been called for as well," Albanese says."You can't oppose the private health insurance changes at the same time as you're calling for changes to fuel taxation, which would have an impact on inflation."
"A range of savings that we have put forward have been rejected by the Coalition, and a range of expenditures have been called for as well," Albanese says.
"You can't oppose the private health insurance changes at the same time as you're calling for changes to fuel taxation, which would have an impact on inflation."
The prime minister says the government won't "rip money" out of health or schools.
"We're trying to find savings as well in order to fund aged care going forward. My government will continue to look for all of those measures."

Albanese says he doesn't accept govt policies have led to rate rise
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says he doesn't accept that his government's policies led to yesterday's interest rate rise.
The Reserve Bank hiked interest rates for the fifth time this year to 4.85 per cent. It's the highest cash rate since late 2008.
The latest Final Budget Outcome showed government spending had grown to 26.9 per cent of gross domestic product.
Albanese says the Reserve Bank's governor has spoken about international pressures on the budget.

"Regularly she has spoken about international pressures as well as domestic demand. That's something that we don't disagree with," Albanese says."I didn't see the press conference but I'm sure that Michelle Bullock would have not acknowledged that oil prices have had an impact."
"Regularly she has spoken about international pressures as well as domestic demand. That's something that we don't disagree with," Albanese says.
"I didn't see the press conference but I'm sure that Michelle Bullock would have not acknowledged that oil prices have had an impact."
PM says he held 'constructive' talks with Burnham on backpackers
Anthony Albanese says he advocated for a change to the Australia-UK free trade agreement in relation to backpackers with the UK prime minister.
Currently, the UK free trade deal allows British backpackers to stay in Australia for up to three years without requiring specific work to be undertaken.
The federal government wants to change the rules for those backpackers so that Labor can reduce its net overseas migration number.
The prime minister says he had a "constructive" discussion with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham about the matter.

"He was very constructive about it and we tasked our officials to do further work," Albanese says."There are options that we discussed. We'll discuss it diplomatically. That's how you get things done and it was a positive reception, from from Prime Minister Burnham."
"He was very constructive about it and we tasked our officials to do further work," Albanese says.
"There are options that we discussed. We'll discuss it diplomatically. That's how you get things done and it was a positive reception, from from Prime Minister Burnham."
Albanese holds press conference in Antigua following meetings with Burnham, Carney
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has just stepped up to give a press conference in Antigua, where he is attending the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM).
Albanese says discussions have been "really productive" and have focused on the international economy and trade.
He says he had a successful and positive meeting with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, where they discussed the progress of AUKUS.
"Prime Minister Burnham is very supportive of it [AUKUS] and we were able to talk about the progress that is being made," Albanese says.
Albanese says he also met with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, where they discussed defence, critical minerals and trade.
Artificial intelligence was also discussed with both leaders, Albanese says. The Ukraine and Middle East wars were discussed with the wider group of CHOGM leaders, he says.
"It has been an opportunity to renew relationships with people, but also to forge new ones as well," he says.
Rishworth says budget isn't the primary driver of interest rate rise
Workplace Relations Minister Amanda Rishworth has been the first cabinet minister up this morning to be grilled about interest rates.
Speaking to Channel Nine, Rishworth says the government's budget is not the primary driver of yesterday's Reserve Bank interest rate rise.
But she says that won't stop the government from trying to make savings.
"Budgets are not the primary driver here. We of course as a government take responsibility to make sure that ... we are having responsible savings and targeted cost of living relief," Rishworth says.
Taylor defends Coalition opposition to Labor spending cuts
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor has defended the Coalition's opposition to government savings measures following yesterday's interest rate hike.
Yesterday, Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock said overall public and private demand remained too high across the economy.
Speaking to ABC News Breakfast, Taylor says federal government spending is too high and needs to be cut back to reduce demand.

"One of the things driving demand is going much faster than the overall economy is government spending," Taylor says."We've also got an economy that's sclerotic. It's not growing. Enterprise is is giving up the ghost. Small businesses are really struggling."
"One of the things driving demand is going much faster than the overall economy is government spending," Taylor says.
"We've also got an economy that's sclerotic. It's not growing. Enterprise is is giving up the ghost. Small businesses are really struggling."

Asked if the Coalition has any credibility calling for spending cuts when it has opposed savings measures such as a private health insurance rebate for over 65s, Taylor says it's overall spending that matters.
"It's aggregate spending that matters ... the overall spending that drives inflation and, look, we know this. The IMF is saying that spending is too high."
